def-csm-frontier-local-topologies.definition_interface:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a finite nonempty alphabet $S$ with the discrete topology, and a bijective enumeration $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ of $\mathbb Z^d$. Let $\Omega=S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ be the set of all configurations $\sigma:\mathbb Z^d\to S$ with the product topology, the smallest topology that makes each coordinate map $\sigma\mapsto\sigma_x$ continuous. For a finite set $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and assignment $a\in S^F$, the cylinder set determined by $(F,a)$ is $[F,a]=\{\sigma\in\Omega:\sigma|_F=a\}$. The cylinder sigma-algebra $\mathcal C$ is generated by these sets.

For each finite $F$, let $\pi_F:\Omega\to S^F$ be restriction to $F$. A probability measure $\rho$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal C)$ is a countably additive map $\mathcal C\to[0,1]$ with $\rho(\varnothing)=0$ and $\rho(\Omega)=1$. Its finite-coordinate pushforward is the measure on all subsets of $S^F$ defined by $(\pi_F)_*\rho(B):=\rho(\pi_F^{-1}(B))$; the preimage is a finite union of cylinders and belongs to $\mathcal C$. For probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on this space, local weak convergence $\mu_n\to_{\mathrm{loc}}\mu$ means that $(\pi_F)_*\mu_n(B)\to(\pi_F)_*\mu(B)$ for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and every $B\subseteq S^F$. Equivalently, all finite-coordinate cylinder probabilities converge. The cylinder sigma-algebra is shown below in a local result to equal the Borel sigma-algebra, with local weak convergence equal to ordinary weak convergence on this space.

def-csm-frontier-vague-topology.definition_interface:
Fix $d\ge1$. Let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, and understand all measures below as defined on $(\mathbb R^d,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d))$. A measure here is a countably additive map from $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ to $[0,\infty]$ that assigns $0$ to the empty set. A locally finite counting measure on $\mathbb R^d$ is a measure of the form $\xi=\sum_{r\in I}\delta_{x_r}$, where $I$ is finite or countable, repetitions among the points $x_r\in\mathbb R^d$ are allowed, and every compact set contains only finitely many listed points, counting repetitions. The empty sum is allowed and is the zero measure. For a Borel set $B$, $\xi(B)$ is the number of listed points in $B$, with multiplicity. Write $\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$ for the set of these measures. For $x\in\mathbb R^d$, the point mass $\delta_x$ assigns mass $1$ to a Borel set containing $x$ and mass $0$ otherwise.

For any continuous compactly supported $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ and $\xi=\sum_{r\in I}\delta_{x_r}$, define $\int f\,d\xi:=\sum_{r:x_r\in\operatorname{supp}f}f(x_r)$, where $\operatorname{supp}f$ is the closure of $\{x:f(x)\ne0\}$. This sum is finite by local finiteness, counts multiplicities, and is independent of the listing because $\xi$ fixes the multiplicity at every point. For the zero measure it is $0$.

The vague topology on $\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$ is the coarsest topology for which $\xi\mapsto\int f\,d\xi$ is continuous for every nonnegative continuous compactly supported function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$. Thus $\xi_n\to_{\mathrm v}\xi$ exactly when $\int f\,d\xi_n\to\int f\,d\xi$ for every such $f$.

Given a probability space $(\Theta,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$, meaning that $\mathcal A$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Theta$ and $\mathbb P$ is a countably additive probability measure on $\mathcal A$ with $\mathbb P(\Theta)=1$, a random locally finite counting measure is an $(\mathcal A,\mathcal B_{\mathrm v})$-measurable map $\Xi:\Theta\to\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$, where $\mathcal B_{\mathrm v}:=\sigma\{U:U\text{ is open in the vague topology just defined}\}$. We require that, for every bounded Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the evaluation $\Xi(B):\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ given by $\Xi(B)(\theta)=\Xi(\theta)(B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable; it is finite by local finiteness. Write $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}$ for integration with respect to $\mathbb P$. A sequence $(\Xi_n)$ of such measures on a common probability space uses this same domain and target for every $n$. If $K$ is compact, its local counts are uniformly integrable on $K$ when

$$\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_n\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\!\left[\Xi_n(K)\mathbf1_{\{\Xi_n(K)>R\}}\right]=0.$$

This is the count-tail condition used when an argument needs control of unbounded observables supported in $K$. The definition asserts no convergence of expectations without the exact test-function, support, and tail hypotheses of the result being applied.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

$$D(p\|q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i},&p_i>0\Rightarrow q_i>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Then $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a finite nonempty alphabet $S$ with the discrete topology, and a bijective enumeration $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ of $\mathbb Z^d$. Let $\Omega=S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ be the set of all configurations $\sigma:\mathbb Z^d\to S$ with the product topology, the smallest topology that makes each coordinate map $\sigma\mapsto\sigma_x$ continuous. For a finite set $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and assignment $a\in S^F$, the cylinder set determined by $(F,a)$ is $[F,a]=\{\sigma\in\Omega:\sigma|_F=a\}$. The cylinder sigma-algebra $\mathcal C$ is generated by these sets.

For each finite $F$, let $\pi_F:\Omega\to S^F$ be restriction to $F$. A probability measure $\rho$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal C)$ is a countably additive map $\mathcal C\to[0,1]$ with $\rho(\varnothing)=0$ and $\rho(\Omega)=1$. Its finite-coordinate pushforward is the measure on all subsets of $S^F$ defined by $(\pi_F)_*\rho(B):=\rho(\pi_F^{-1}(B))$; the preimage is a finite union of cylinders and belongs to $\mathcal C$. For probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on this space, local weak convergence $\mu_n\to_{\mathrm{loc}}\mu$ means that $(\pi_F)_*\mu_n(B)\to(\pi_F)_*\mu(B)$ for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and every $B\subseteq S^F$. Equivalently, all finite-coordinate cylinder probabilities converge. The cylinder sigma-algebra is shown below in a local result to equal the Borel sigma-algebra, with local weak convergence equal to ordinary weak convergence on this space.

derivations.claim: If $\sigma\ne\eta$, some coordinate differs, so $\rho(\sigma,\eta)>0$; symmetry is immediate, and the coordinatewise triangle inequality gives the triangle inequality after summing. If two configurations agree on $x_1,\ldots,x_N$, then $\rho\le\sum_{k>N}2^{-k}=2^{-N}$. Conversely, if $\rho(\sigma,\eta)<2^{-N}$, no coordinate among $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ differs, because a mismatch at $x_k$ contributes at least $2^{-N}$. These bounds show that metric balls and finite-coordinate basic neighborhoods generate the same topology.

If $\mu_n\to_{\mathrm{loc}}\mu$, every cylinder indicator is bounded and continuous by [F2], so its integrals converge. Every bounded function depending on finitely many coordinates is a finite linear combination of cylinder indicators, and its integrals therefore converge as well.

Suppose an open cover of $\Omega$ has no finite subcover. Let $C_0=\Omega$. Recursively, if $C_{N-1}$ is the cylinder fixing the first $N-1$ spins and has no finite subcover, its finitely many children obtained by assigning $\sigma_{x_N}=s$ cannot all have finite subcovers; otherwise their finite union would cover $C_{N-1}$. Choose the least $s$ in the fixed order whose child still has no finite subcover and call that child $C_N$. These nested cylinders determine a configuration $\sigma$. A cover member containing $\sigma$ contains a basic neighborhood fixing finitely many sites; for sufficiently large $N$, $C_N$ lies inside that neighborhood and hence has a one-member subcover, a contradiction. Thus every open cover has a finite subcover and $\Omega$ is compact.

Each cylinder is clopen by [F2], and cylinders form a countable basis: $\mathbb Z^d$ has countably many finite subsets, and each finite coordinate set has finitely many spin assignments. Therefore every open set is a countable union of cylinders and belongs to the cylinder sigma-algebra, while every cylinder is Borel. Hence the two sigma-algebras are equal.

Fix a bounded continuous $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. For each $\sigma$, continuity and the cylinder basis give a cylinder neighborhood $C_\sigma$ of $\sigma$ on which $|g(\eta)-g(\sigma)|<\varepsilon/3$. Compactness from step 2.1 gives a finite subcover $C_1,\ldots,C_r$. Let $F$ be the union of the finitely many coordinate sets fixed by these cylinders. If $\eta,\zeta$ agree on $F$, choose a $C_i$ containing $\eta$; because $C_i$ depends only on a subset of $F$, it also contains $\zeta$, so $|g(\eta)-g(\zeta)|<2\varepsilon/3$. Choose $N$ with $F\subseteq\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}$ and fix one default spin $s_0\in S$. Replace all coordinates after $x_N$ by $s_0$ to define a canonical extension $\widehat\sigma$ of each first-$N$ prefix, and set $g_N(\sigma)=g(\widehat\sigma)$. Then $g_N$ depends only on the first $N$ coordinates and $\sup_\sigma|g(\sigma)-g_N(\sigma)|<\varepsilon$.

For every $n$, $|\int g\,d\mu_n-\int g_N\,d\mu_n|\le\varepsilon$ and the same bound holds for $\mu$. Step 1.2 gives $\int g_N\,d\mu_n\to\int g_N\,d\mu$, so the limit superior of $|\int g\,d\mu_n-\int g\,d\mu|$ is at most $2\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, weak convergence follows. Conversely, if $\mu_n$ converges weakly, indicators of all cylinders are bounded continuous by [F2], so their probabilities converge; finite sums give every finite marginal, hence local weak convergence by [F1].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $E=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for a finite integer $m\ge1$. A rate matrix on $E$ is a real matrix $L=(L_{ij})_{i,j\in E}$ such that $L_{ij}\ge0$ for $i
e j$ and $\sum_{j\in E}L_{ij}=0$ for every $i$. Write $\lambda_i=\sum_{j
e i}L_{ij}$, so $L_{ii}=-\lambda_i$. The row convention acts on a column observable $f:E	o\mathbb R$ by $(Lf)(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}f(j)$; a row probability vector evolves by right multiplication.

Fix an initial probability vector $
u=(
u_i)_{i\in E}$, meaning $
u_i\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in E}
u_i=1$; initial law $
u$ means $\mathbb P(Y_0=i)=
u_i$ for every $i\in E$. Put $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, then $L=0$ and set $N_t=0$ for every $t\ge0$ and let the associated realization be the constant process $X_t=Y_0$ with $Y_0\sim
u$. If $q>0$, put $R=I+L/q$, a stochastic matrix. A uniformized realization consists of a probability space carrying a discrete-time Markov sequence $(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ with initial law $
u$ and transition matrix $R$, and independent random variables $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ that are independent of the entire sequence $Y$ and satisfy $\mathbb P(W_n>u)=e^{-qu}$ for $u\ge0$. Here a discrete-time Markov sequence with transition matrix $R$ means that
$$\mathbb P(A\cap\{Y_{n+1}=j\})=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_{Y_nj}]$$
for every $n\ge0$, $j\in E$, and $A\in\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)$. Each $W_n$ therefore has the exponential distribution of rate $q$; in particular its mean is $q^{-1}$. Require $\sum_{n\ge1}W_n=+\infty$ almost surely. Put $T_0=0$, $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nW_k$, and, on this probability-one event, $N_t=\max\{n:T_n\le t\}$ and $X_t=Y_{N_t}$. On its null complement set $N_t=0$ and $X_t=Y_0$. The construction filtration is $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(N_s,X_s:0\le s\le t)$; it records event counts and states through time $t$ and is not completed or made right-continuous by this definition.

This uniformized construction permits reducible rate matrices and states with zero exit rate. Under the Axiom of Choice, [[lem-csm-frontier-finite-generator-chain-existence]] proves that every finite rate matrix and initial law admit such a realization and that its conditional transition matrices are $e^{tL}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^nL^n/n!$.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. derivations.claim: Put $\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}L_{ij}$ and $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, all off-diagonal entries vanish and the zero row sums force $L=0$. On the finite probability space $(E,2^E,\nu)$ put $Y_0(\omega)=\omega$ and $X_t=Y_0$ for all $t$. Then $N_t=0$, paths are constant, the conditional transition is the identity, and $e^{tL}=I$, giving the conclusion in this case.

Suppose $q>0$. For $i\ne j$, $R_{ij}=L_{ij}/q\ge0$, while $R_{ii}=1-\lambda_i/q\ge0$; each row sums to $1$. Let $\mu_q(dw)=q e^{-qw}\,dw$ on $(0,\infty)$, a probability measure because its density integrates to $1$. On $E\times(0,\infty)$ use initial law $\nu\otimes\mu_q$ and transition kernel $K((i,w),\{j\}\times B)=R_{ij}\mu_q(B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq(0,\infty)$. For any Borel subset of the product, its kernel value is the finite sum over $j$ of $R_{ij}$ times the $\mu_q$-measure of the corresponding section; thus it is measurable, nonnegative and has total mass $1$.

Apply [F2] to this initial law and kernel, and write the resulting coordinates as $Z_n=(Y_n,W_{n+1})$. Their finite-prefix law factors as the Markov-chain prefix law for $Y$ times $\prod_{k=1}^{n+1}\mu_q(dW_k)$, because every transition kernel chooses the next state with probabilities $R_{ij}$ and the next waiting time with the same factor $\mu_q$, independently of the current waiting time. Cylinder events generate the two coordinate sigma-algebras, so [F3] extends this factorization to independence of the full sequence $Y$ from the iid family $(W_k)$. The first coordinate is an $R$-Markov sequence with initial law $\nu$, as required by [F1].

Each $W_k$ has probability $e^{-1}$ of being at least $q^{-1}$. For any fixed $r$, independence gives $\mathbb P(W_k<q^{-1}\text{ for }r\le k\le n)=(1-e^{-1})^{n-r+1}\to0$. Continuity of probability for decreasing events, obtained by applying [F4] to complements, shows that the probability of no such event after $r$ is zero. A countable union over $r$ shows that $W_k\ge q^{-1}$ occurs infinitely often almost surely, and therefore $\sum_kW_k=\infty$ almost surely. On every bounded time interval there are consequently finitely many event times; the convention $X_t=Y_{N_t}$ makes paths right-continuous with left limits.

For $n\ge1$, convolution of the exponential densities gives the arrival-time density $$ f_{T_n}(u)=\frac{q^n u^{n-1}e^{-qu}}{(n-1)!},\qquad u>0. $$ Indeed the formula holds for $n=1$, and convolving it with $q e^{-q(t-u)}$ gives $q^{n+1}e^{-qt}\int_0^t u^{n-1}du/(n-1)!=q^{n+1}t^ne^{-qt}/n!$. Since $W_{n+1}$ is independent of $T_n$, for $n\ge1$, $$ \mathbb P(N_t=n)=\int_0^t f_{T_n}(u)\mathbb P(W_{n+1}>t-u)\,du=e^{-qt}\frac{(qt)^n}{n!}; $$ for $n=0$ the probability is $\mathbb P(W_1>t)=e^{-qt}$.

The event process has independent rate-$q$ Poisson increments. To see the conditional assertion needed here, on $\{N_s=n\}$ the event-clock history gives $T_n\le s<T_{n+1}$; by the exponential memoryless identity $\mathbb P(W_{n+1}-(s-T_n)>u\mid W_{n+1}>s-T_n)=e^{-qu}$, the residual time after $s$ is rate-$q$ exponential independent of that history. The later waiting times are independent rate-$q$ exponentials as well. Repeating the calculation in step 3.2 shows that, conditional on the clock history up to $s$, $N_{s+h}-N_s$ has probabilities $e^{-qh}(qh)^k/k!$, independent of that history. The clock is independent of $Y$ by step 2.1 and the uniformized convention [F1].

Let $H_s=(Y_0,\ldots,Y_{N_s})$ be the finite embedded-state prefix and put $\mathcal G_s=\sigma(N_u:0\le u\le s,H_s)$. Since $N_u\le N_s$ for $u\le s$, the construction filtration $\mathcal F_s=\sigma(N_u,X_u:0\le u\le s)$ is contained in $\mathcal G_s$. Given $\mathcal G_s$ and $X_s=i$, $k$ further clock events have probability $e^{-qh}(qh)^k/k!$ by step 4.1, and the embedded chain has $k$-step transition matrix $R^k$. Hence $$ \mathbb P(X_{s+h}=j\mid\mathcal G_s)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-qh}\frac{(qh)^k}{k!}(R^k)_{ij}=\bigl(e^{-qh}e^{qhR}\bigr)_{ij}=(e^{hL})_{ij}, $$ since $q(R-I)=L$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $E=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for a finite integer $m\ge1$. A rate matrix on $E$ is a real matrix $L=(L_{ij})_{i,j\in E}$ such that $L_{ij}\ge0$ for $i
e j$ and $\sum_{j\in E}L_{ij}=0$ for every $i$. Write $\lambda_i=\sum_{j
e i}L_{ij}$, so $L_{ii}=-\lambda_i$. The row convention acts on a column observable $f:E	o\mathbb R$ by $(Lf)(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}f(j)$; a row probability vector evolves by right multiplication.

Fix an initial probability vector $
u=(
u_i)_{i\in E}$, meaning $
u_i\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in E}
u_i=1$; initial law $
u$ means $\mathbb P(Y_0=i)=
u_i$ for every $i\in E$. Put $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, then $L=0$ and set $N_t=0$ for every $t\ge0$ and let the associated realization be the constant process $X_t=Y_0$ with $Y_0\sim
u$. If $q>0$, put $R=I+L/q$, a stochastic matrix. A uniformized realization consists of a probability space carrying a discrete-time Markov sequence $(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ with initial law $
u$ and transition matrix $R$, and independent random variables $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ that are independent of the entire sequence $Y$ and satisfy $\mathbb P(W_n>u)=e^{-qu}$ for $u\ge0$. Here a discrete-time Markov sequence with transition matrix $R$ means that
$$\mathbb P(A\cap\{Y_{n+1}=j\})=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_{Y_nj}]$$
for every $n\ge0$, $j\in E$, and $A\in\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)$. Each $W_n$ therefore has the exponential distribution of rate $q$; in particular its mean is $q^{-1}$. Require $\sum_{n\ge1}W_n=+\infty$ almost surely. Put $T_0=0$, $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nW_k$, and, on this probability-one event, $N_t=\max\{n:T_n\le t\}$ and $X_t=Y_{N_t}$. On its null complement set $N_t=0$ and $X_t=Y_0$. The construction filtration is $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(N_s,X_s:0\le s\le t)$; it records event counts and states through time $t$ and is not completed or made right-continuous by this definition.

This uniformized construction permits reducible rate matrices and states with zero exit rate. Under the Axiom of Choice, [[lem-csm-frontier-finite-generator-chain-existence]] proves that every finite rate matrix and initial law admit such a realization and that its conditional transition matrices are $e^{tL}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^nL^n/n!$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E$ be a nonempty finite set, let $L$ be a rate matrix on $E$ with nonnegative off-diagonal entries and zero row sums, and let $\nu$ be an initial probability vector. Then there exists a uniformized realization under the conventions stated below. Its paths are càdlàg and almost surely have only finitely many event times on each bounded interval (nonexplosion), and, for all $0\le s\le t$,
$$\mathbb P(X_t=j\mid\mathcal F_s)=(e^{(t-s)L})_{X_sj}\quad\text{almost surely},$$
where $\mathcal F_s=\sigma(N_u,X_u:0\le u\le s)$ is the construction filtration. In particular, $e^{tL}$ is the transition matrix from any initial state.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $D=(D_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a continuous martingale relative to a
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)$, with $D_0=0$. Suppose each path has finite total
variation $V_T(D)$ and $\mathbb E V_T(D)<\infty$. Then $D$ is indistinguishably
zero on $[0,T]$.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], for $h\ge0$ and $g=Lf$, $\mathbb E[g(X_{s+r})\mid\mathcal F_s]=(e^{rL}g)(X_s)$. The paths are piecewise constant with finitely many jumps on bounded intervals, so the bounded integrand is jointly measurable and [F5] applies. Testing against each event in $\mathcal F_s$ gives $$ \mathbb E\!\left[\int_s^{s+h}g(X_u)\,du\middle|\mathcal F_s\right] =\int_0^h(e^{rL}Lf)(X_s)\,dr=(e^{hL}f-f)(X_s), $$ where the last equality follows by termwise differentiation of the absolutely convergent finite-matrix exponential series. Also $\mathbb E[f(X_{s+h})\mid\mathcal F_s]=(e^{hL}f)(X_s)$. Subtracting proves $\mathbb E[M_{s+h}-M_s\mid\mathcal F_s]=0$ for every $s,h$. On $[0,T]$, $|M_t|\le2\|f\|_\infty+T\|Lf\|_\infty$, so every $M_t$ is square-integrable and the all-pairs martingale assertion follows from [F2].

Since $\sum_jL_{ij}=0$, $$ \Gamma_f(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}(f(j)-f(i))^2=\sum_{j\ne i}L_{ij}(f(j)-f(i))^2\ge0. $$ Thus $A$ is increasing and bounded on $[0,T]$. It is adapted because it is the time integral of the bounded adapted process $\Gamma_f(X_s)$. It is continuous. For each $n$, the step process equal to $A_{kT/2^n}$ on $(kT/2^n,(k+1)T/2^n]$ and zero at time zero is predictable by [F4]; these processes converge pointwise to $A$ by continuity. Therefore $A$ is predictable.

Fix $u$ and condition on $\mathcal F_u$, writing $X_u=i$. For $0<h\le1$, the number of uniformization events during $(u,u+h]$ is Poisson with rate $q=\max_i\lambda_i$ by the exponential-clock construction in [F1]. If there is no event, $\Delta M:=M_{u+h}-M_u=-h g(i)$, whose square is $O(h^2)$. If there is exactly one event and the new state is $j\ne i$, its probability is $e^{-qh}qhR_{ij}=e^{-qh}hL_{ij}=hL_{ij}+O(h^2)$, and $\Delta M=f(j)-f(i)+O(h)$ uniformly because the drift integral has magnitude at most $h\|g\|_\infty$. Its contribution to the conditional second moment is therefore $hL_{ij}(f(j)-f(i))^2+O(h^2)$. A one-event self-transition contributes $O(h^3)$. The probability of at least two events is $O(h^2)$ and $\Delta M$ is uniformly bounded for $h\le1$, so its contribution is $O(h^2)$. Since $E$ is finite, all error bounds are uniform in $i$, and $$ \mathbb E[(\Delta M)^2\mid\mathcal F_u]=h\Gamma_f(i)+O(h^2). $$ Also $\mathbb P(X_{u+r}\ne i\mid\mathcal F_u)\le qr$, so boundedness of $\Gamma_f$ gives $$ \mathbb E\!\left[\int_u^{u+h}\Gamma_f(X_v)\,dv\middle|\mathcal F_u\right]=h\Gamma_f(i)+O(h^2). $$ Consequently $\left|\mathbb E[(\Delta M)^2-\int_u^{u+h}\Gamma_f(X_v)\,dv\mid\mathcal F_u]\right|\le C h^2$ for a finite constant $C$ depending only on $L,f,T$.

Let $D_t=M_t^2-A_t$. On any interval $[u,u+h]$, $D_{u+h}-D_u=2M_u\Delta M+(\Delta M)^2-\int_u^{u+h}\Gamma_f(X_v)\,dv$. On $[0,T]$, $M_u$ is bounded and $\mathcal F_u$-measurable by step 1.1, so [F7] and the mean-zero increment give $\mathbb E[2M_u\Delta M\mid\mathcal F_u]=2M_u\mathbb E[\Delta M\mid\mathcal F_u]=0$, while step 2.1 bounds the conditional expectation of the remaining terms by $Ch^2$. For fixed $s<t$, divide $[s,t]$ into $n$ equal intervals of length $h=(t-s)/n\le1$. For the subdivision times $u$, $\mathcal F_s\subseteq\mathcal F_u$ and every increment of $D$ is integrable. Thus [F8], linearity and order in [F3], and the preceding bound imply $|\mathbb E[D_t-D_s\mid\mathcal F_s]|\le nCh^2=C(t-s)^2/n$. Letting $n\to\infty$ proves $\mathbb E[D_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=D_s$. Thus $M^2-A$ is a martingale.

In this item, a continuous predictable bracket means a continuous predictable increasing process $B$ with $B_0=0$, $\mathbb E B_T<\infty$, and $M^2-B$ a martingale. Steps 1.2 and 3.1 show that $A$ has these properties. If $B$ is another such process, then $B-A$ is a continuous martingale starting at zero, and its total variation on $[0,T]$ is at most $B_T+A_T$, which is integrable. By [F6], $B-A$ is indistinguishably zero. Therefore $A$ is the unique bracket in this stated continuous predictable compensator class, and it has the displayed formula.

Joint measurability follows from right-continuous step paths by deterministic right-grid approximations; on [0,t] these use values no later than t, proving adaptedness of the drift integrals. Fubini applies to bounded functions on finite Lebesgue time times probability. Uniform finite-matrix exponential differentiation gives the drift identity and deterministic L2 bound. Gamma is the nonnegative rate-weighted squared-jump sum. Dyadic left-step approximations to continuous adapted A prove predictability. Independent clock increments and embedded transitions give uniform O(h^2) errors in every state; the zero/self/multiple-event cases are covered. Fix $d\ge1$. Let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, and understand all measures below as defined on $(\mathbb R^d,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d))$. A measure here is a countably additive map from $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ to $[0,\infty]$ that assigns $0$ to the empty set. A locally finite counting measure on $\mathbb R^d$ is a measure of the form $\xi=\sum_{r\in I}\delta_{x_r}$, where $I$ is finite or countable, repetitions among the points $x_r\in\mathbb R^d$ are allowed, and every compact set contains only finitely many listed points, counting repetitions. The empty sum is allowed and is the zero measure. For a Borel set $B$, $\xi(B)$ is the number of listed points in $B$, with multiplicity. Write $\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$ for the set of these measures. For $x\in\mathbb R^d$, the point mass $\delta_x$ assigns mass $1$ to a Borel set containing $x$ and mass $0$ otherwise.

For any continuous compactly supported $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ and $\xi=\sum_{r\in I}\delta_{x_r}$, define $\int f\,d\xi:=\sum_{r:x_r\in\operatorname{supp}f}f(x_r)$, where $\operatorname{supp}f$ is the closure of $\{x:f(x)\ne0\}$. This sum is finite by local finiteness, counts multiplicities, and is independent of the listing because $\xi$ fixes the multiplicity at every point. For the zero measure it is $0$.

The vague topology on $\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$ is the coarsest topology for which $\xi\mapsto\int f\,d\xi$ is continuous for every nonnegative continuous compactly supported function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$. Thus $\xi_n\to_{\mathrm v}\xi$ exactly when $\int f\,d\xi_n\to\int f\,d\xi$ for every such $f$.

Given a probability space $(\Theta,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$, meaning that $\mathcal A$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Theta$ and $\mathbb P$ is a countably additive probability measure on $\mathcal A$ with $\mathbb P(\Theta)=1$, a random locally finite counting measure is an $(\mathcal A,\mathcal B_{\mathrm v})$-measurable map $\Xi:\Theta\to\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$, where $\mathcal B_{\mathrm v}:=\sigma\{U:U\text{ is open in the vague topology just defined}\}$. We require that, for every bounded Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the evaluation $\Xi(B):\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ given by $\Xi(B)(\theta)=\Xi(\theta)(B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable; it is finite by local finiteness. Write $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}$ for integration with respect to $\mathbb P$. A sequence $(\Xi_n)$ of such measures on a common probability space uses this same domain and target for every $n$. If $K$ is compact, its local counts are uniformly integrable on $K$ when

$$\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_n\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\!\left[\Xi_n(K)\mathbf1_{\{\Xi_n(K)>R\}}\right]=0.$$

This is the count-tail condition used when an argument needs control of unbounded observables supported in $K$. The definition asserts no convergence of expectations without the exact test-function, support, and tail hypotheses of the result being applied.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a finite nonempty alphabet $S$ with the discrete topology, and a bijective enumeration $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ of $\mathbb Z^d$. Let $\Omega=S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ be the set of all configurations $\sigma:\mathbb Z^d\to S$ with the product topology, the smallest topology that makes each coordinate map $\sigma\mapsto\sigma_x$ continuous. For a finite set $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and assignment $a\in S^F$, the cylinder set determined by $(F,a)$ is $[F,a]=\{\sigma\in\Omega:\sigma|_F=a\}$. The cylinder sigma-algebra $\mathcal C$ is generated by these sets.

For each finite $F$, let $\pi_F:\Omega\to S^F$ be restriction to $F$. A probability measure $\rho$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal C)$ is a countably additive map $\mathcal C\to[0,1]$ with $\rho(\varnothing)=0$ and $\rho(\Omega)=1$. Its finite-coordinate pushforward is the measure on all subsets of $S^F$ defined by $(\pi_F)_*\rho(B):=\rho(\pi_F^{-1}(B))$; the preimage is a finite union of cylinders and belongs to $\mathcal C$. For probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on this space, local weak convergence $\mu_n\to_{\mathrm{loc}}\mu$ means that $(\pi_F)_*\mu_n(B)\to(\pi_F)_*\mu(B)$ for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and every $B\subseteq S^F$. Equivalently, all finite-coordinate cylinder probabilities converge. The cylinder sigma-algebra is shown below in a local result to equal the Borel sigma-algebra, with local weak convergence equal to ordinary weak convergence on this space.

derivations.claim: For any fixed site $x\in S_n$, exactly $(2n-1)!$ of the $(2n)!$ bijections send label $1$ to $x$. Thus $U_n$ is uniform on $S_n$ under $\mathbb P_n$. The inverse label $\pi_n^{-1}(0)$ is also uniform on $L_n$, because exactly $(2n-1)!$ bijections assign any prescribed label to site $0$. Exactly $n$ labels carry each mark, so $\mathbb P_n(V_n=0)=\mathbb P_n(V_n=1)=1/2$.

Let $K=\operatorname{supp}f$. Since $K$ is compact, it is bounded and $K\cap\mathbb Z$ is finite; write $c_K=|K\cap\mathbb Z|$. Uniformity of $U_n$ gives $\mathbb P_n(U_n\in K)=|K\cap S_n|/(2n)\le c_K/(2n)$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, [F1] gives
$$\mathbb P_n\!\left(\left|\int f\,d\Xi_n\right|>\varepsilon\right)\le\mathbb P_n(U_n\in K)\le\frac{c_K}{2n}\longrightarrow0.$$
Thus each compactly supported vague test tends to zero in probability, while step 1.1 shows that selecting by the fixed spatial site $0$ retains a nondegenerate mark law. This is a statement about spatial point-measure tests; finite-coordinate local convergence on spin configurations is a separate notion by [F2]. These two statements concern different selection rules and do not contradict one another.
